concepts.title: Policy, offers and a client lease
concepts.text: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) supplies a client address, subnet mask and options such as a router and DNS-server addresses. Applied policy describes future offers. concepts.title: Apply is not a renewal
concepts.text: Apply changes policy only. A client can still hold its older router and DNS values. A manual Renew can take current policy even before the usual T1 time when the held address remains eligible. If the server cannot extend that address under current policy, it can acknowledge the old grant without changing its options or expiry. Inspect the actual result.

concepts.title: Renew or obtain a new grant
concepts.text: T1 marks the usual scheduled renewal time. Advance changes the explicit simulated clock only; it never sends a request. The worked example waits until T1 and chooses Renew using supplied unicast reachability. A manual earlier Renew is also valid when the address remains eligible. Alternatively Release stops client use, then Discover and Request obtain a new grant. Expiry also ends client use.

concepts.title: An address finds a computer; a port finds an application

concepts.title: TCP opens a two-way conversation

TCP provides an ordered byte stream in real systems; this small model demonstrates the opening and one supplied fragment, not retransmission or congestion control.

concepts.text: UDP does not use the TCP handshake. The sensor sends one supplied datagram. The trace distinguishes sending, delivery to a host and receipt by a matching UDP listener. No reply or successful delivery is guaranteed by UDP itself.

goal: Distinguish an address limit from an explicit approved source, then prove the desk remains useful.
context: Builds on VLAN membership and Ethernet source learning; review the earlier handovers if these are new.

concepts.title: A switch learns a source, not a promise
concepts.text: The earlier Ethernet unit showed source learning. A secure port can also learn the first source it sees, up to a maximum. Maximum one means one address, not necessarily the address you intended. If the unexpected sender is first, it can occupy that slot. If that has already happened, Shut down the desk port to clear its learned secure addresses, apply the intended binding, then Bring up.

concepts.title: Name the approved source when arrival order must not decide
concepts.text: A configured secure address reserves a place for that source. In the worked network, sample-desk uses 02:00:00:00:00:15. With maximum one and that configured address, the unrecognized 02:00:00:00:00:1d has no free slot, even if it sends first.

concepts.title: Rejecting a source should not defeat the task
concepts.text: Protect drops the unwanted frame without counting it. Restrict also counts it. Shutdown disables the whole port, including approved traffic. This task needs continued approved traffic, so compare the first two modes rather than disabling the attachment.

concepts.title: Read admission and delivery separately
concepts.text: Send frame supplies one virtual frame from the selected workstation attachment. Source MAC lets you try a different sender on that attachment; it does not change the workstation NIC address shown in the diagram. Admitted means the source passed the policy. Received by names the virtual NICs that actually accepted the destination.

concepts.title: A MAC address is not authentication
concepts.text: A sender that copies an approved source address can pass a MAC filter. Port security is a useful local restriction, not a password check or proof of who owns a device. These frames, tables and settings exist only inside the simulator.

concepts.title: Review the two kinds of secure entry

concepts.title: Compare the violation responses

concepts.title: A replay source is one frame, not a new NIC

Changing Source MAC does not invent a second receiving workstation or change the topology NIC address. No shared-hub, phone or voice-VLAN behavior is simulated.

concepts.text: The worked desk has a retired configured address, and the current workstation triggered shutdown mode. The displayed Error-disabled state is a latch. Repairing the address does not make that latch disappear.

concepts.title: Repair the policy before recovery

concepts.title: Recover explicitly
concepts.text: Use Shut down, then Bring up. Down clears dynamic secure learning and leaves the port administratively down; Up restores it. Configured entries and counters remain. Merely pressing Bring up on an already-Up but error-disabled port is not this recovery sequence.

concepts.title: Verify the repair in both directions

concepts.title: Keep the boundary clear

goal: Protect address offers without blocking the real server, and distinguish an Offer from a recorded lease.
context: Review DHCP Discover/Offer/Request/ACK and Ethernet source addresses if these are new; the earlier units are advisory prerequisites.

concepts.title: Review the initial exchange
concepts.text: A client looks for a server (Discover). The server proposes an address (Offer). The client asks to use it (Request), and the server confirms it (ACK). Snooping observes these messages at the switch; it does not allocate addresses.

concepts.title: Enable the feature and select its VLAN
concepts.text: Enable DHCP snooping for the switch, then include the client’s VLAN in Inspected VLANs. Both are needed. A working exchange alone does not prove that messages were inspected.

concepts.title: Choose where server replies may enter
concepts.text: Ports start untrusted. While inspection is active, a server reply arriving on an untrusted port is rejected. Trust the known server path; keep user-facing ports untrusted. Requests arriving from an untrusted client are sent only toward trusted ports.

concepts.title: Read the address record at the right time
concepts.text: An Offer is a proposal, not confirmation. An observed Request followed by a delivered ACK records the client MAC, address, VLAN, client port and remaining lease time. The record disappears at expiry. A trusted port is a configured allowance, not proof of who owns a device.

worked.label: Enable inspection
worked.explanation: The feature and VLAN selection both apply to the sample client.

worked.label: Select the incoming server path
worked.explanation: Approved replies may enter; user ports cannot inject server replies.

worked.label: Replay the exchange
worked.explanation: The confirmed record belongs to the observed client port and expires after 120 simulated seconds.

practice.observe: The topology supplies the VLAN and server role. Pending edits do not affect messages until applied.

concepts.title: Two places describe the sender
concepts.text: The Ethernet header has a source MAC address. Inside the DHCP message is a client MAC address. In a normal direct client request these match. Read them side by side before deciding why a request passed.

concepts.title: Compare the fields on untrusted ports
concepts.text: Compare the two client MAC fields rejects an untrusted request when those values disagree. It does not replace server-port trust. Repair the comparison, then confirm that the legitimate exchange still works.

concepts.title: Consistency is not authentication
concepts.text: A sender can copy both MAC fields so they agree. This check then permits the request; it does not prove device ownership. The matching-fields sample deliberately does that. Changing replayed sender fields does not change the receiving NIC shown in the topology.

goal: Use confirmed DHCP address records to admit valid ARP and reject unsupported address claims.
context: After DHCP snooping foundations: distinguish a confirmed DHCP address record, an Ethernet frame and an IP address. Introductions remain available when you need a review.

concepts.title: An address claim is not proof
concepts.text: On a local IPv4 network, ARP helps find the Ethernet MAC for an IP address. A request asks who has an address; a reply supplies a mapping. A sender can claim a different IP. These exercises check the claims before delivering frames; they do not run a host ARP cache or ping.

concepts.title: Use a confirmed record
concepts.text: DHCP snooping records a delivered ACK after the client Request. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) can compare an incoming ARP sender’s IP and MAC with that current record in its VLAN. Every replay here first observes that Request/ACK, then sends the named ARP sample.

concepts.title: Choose where inspection applies
concepts.text: Enter the VLAN under Inspect ARP in VLANs. Keep user-facing ports inspected. Bypass ARP inspection exempts incoming traffic on a trusted path; DHCP-server trust is a separate setting. The supplied server does not obtain a client lease, so its replies need an appropriate allowance.

concepts.title: Check both delivery and rejection
concepts.text: A valid claim should reach its intended recipients. Other supplied claims must be rejected. Expiry removes the DHCP record, so an old claim must stop passing. Check work evaluates all these cases separately; a successful ordinary exchange alone is not protection.

server: bypass on

worked.explanation: Replay first observes Request/ACK. A valid sender matches both values; expiry removes that authority.

goal: Repair an exact IP/MAC address-list entry and its interaction with DHCP records.
context: After DHCP snooping foundations: distinguish a confirmed DHCP address record, an Ethernet frame and an IP address. Introductions remain available when you need a review.

concepts.title: A static address may have no DHCP record
concepts.text: A workstation configured with a fixed address does not necessarily request a DHCP lease. Its legitimate ARP can therefore fail a binding check. First identify the supplied IP and the actual MAC in the topology; do not solve this by trusting every message from that port.

concepts.title: Permit one sender pair
concepts.text: An ARP address-list rule matches the sender IP and MAC together. A narrow permit can admit the known static sender while other claims still fail. Rules are evaluated in their listed order; an explicit deny wins over a DHCP record. This editor supports exact pairs, not arbitrary wildcard syntax.

concepts.title: Keep the DHCP fallback
concepts.text: Require a matching list rule (skip DHCP records) rejects senders absent from the list. Leave that option off when unlisted DHCP clients should use their confirmed records. A permanent permit for the DHCP client would keep working after expiry; the assignment tests that mistake.

concepts.title: Separate policy from observation
concepts.text: Apply ARP policy changes settings. Replay sample starts its own supplied network, obtains the sample client’s DHCP record, and then tests ARP. Actual replay results report what happened. Check work separately checks every required behavior without replacing the displayed observations.

worked.explanation: Use the static sample workstation’s known IP and actual MAC, rather than the erroneous MAC in the starter.

worked.label: Preserve DHCP fallback
worked.value:
Require a matching list rule:
off
worked.explanation: Unlisted DHCP clients still use current records. A static-only miss would reject them.

worked.label: Explore the boundary
worked.value:
Unexpected static identity
Expired DHCP record
worked.explanation: Both must be rejected. A broad port exemption or a permanent DHCP-client permit would fail these checks.

practice.observe: The list admits the static sender; other DHCP senders can fall back to their current records.

concepts.title: The header and message describe different things

concepts.title: Compare the source fields

concepts.title: A reply knows its target

concepts.title: Preserve legitimate traffic

concepts.title: Match source addresses in order

goal: Configure explicit local identity checks, retain two different access levels and diagnose failed training logins.
context: After Remote management: protocols and approved sources. A workstation’s source IP, a login account and its resulting access level are different things; the Introduction explains each before the assignment.

concepts.title: A computer and an account are different
concepts.text: The source-address policy chooses which workstation may approach the management endpoint. A local account identifies the person signing in. Two people can use the same workstation; an allowed source IP is not proof of a valid account.

concepts.title: Check identity, then choose access
concepts.text: Authentication asks whether an account name and credential match. Authorization decides what access follows. User EXEC level 1 and privileged EXEC level 15 are different. This subset models those two levels and explicit local authorization, without executing a command shell.

concepts.title: Write explicit local settings

The default local-case login method uses case-sensitive local account names; local EXEC authorization uses the matching record’s level. Accounting and remote servers are outside this exercise. Missing method settings are errors, not guessed defaults.

concepts.title: Create records, then test both outcomes

context: After Remote management: protocols and approved sources. A workstation’s source IP, a login account and its resulting access level are different things; the Introduction explains each before the assignment.

concepts.text: A working login is not enough when responsibility changes. Establish the new maintainer’s required access and keep the observer at the lower level. The current incoming IP/protocol policy stays in force throughout.

goal: Repair method order so a responding identity service controls authentication and only an unavailable service leads to local recovery.
context: After Local device access: named accounts and a safe handover. Use the existing incoming policy, named records and levels; the concepts below introduce method order, unavailable versus refused replies, and the separate local authorization decision.

concepts.title: Two places can check an identity
concepts.text: A central training directory and the device’s local records are separate stores. A group NAME method asks the supplied named directory. local-case compares a local record. In this simulator, both stores explicitly use case-sensitive names and supplied training words; this does not implement a real AAA server protocol.

concepts.title: A refusal is different from no answer
concepts.text: An available directory can reply that a name is unknown or its word is wrong. That reply ends authentication. If the directory is unavailable, there is no credential decision, so the next configured method may be tried. Do not treat a wrong word as an outage.

concepts.title: Write the intended order
concepts.text: The line aaa authentication login default group SampleDirectory local-case tries SampleDirectory first and the local store only if that service is unavailable. Reversing the methods makes a local reply finish the check before the directory is consulted. The service state beside each trial is a supplied condition, not a real network measurement.

concepts.title: Identity is followed by an access decision
concepts.text: After authentication, explicit local EXEC authorization looks up the same account name’s local profile and access level. An authenticated central visitor without a permitted local profile is still denied access. User level 1 and privileged level 15 are different; accounting is another function and is not provided by this exercise.

goal: Derive a legacy interface identifier, then restore a complete IPv6 workstation path.
context: Builds on IPv6 workstation addressing, /64 prefixes, link-local next hops and the native address/route editor. The introduction explains the additional hexadecimal-byte and bit-toggle ideas.

concepts.title: Separate the network half from the interface half
concepts.text: For the /64 used here, the first four IPv6 groups name the network and the final four identify an interface. A group holds four hexadecimal digits: 0–9 and a–f. Two digits make one byte (8 bits). A six-byte MAC contains 48 bits; this legacy method turns it into a 64-bit interface identifier.

concepts.title: Insert two bytes, then toggle one bit
concepts.text: Split the MAC after its third byte and insert ff:fe. Next invert the bit with value 2 (second from the right) in the first original byte. 0x02 means hexadecimal 02; XOR 02 flips only that bit. Toggle means 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0: it does not mean always add 2. For example 00 becomes 02, while 0a becomes 08. The other seven identifier bytes stay in order.

concepts.title: Regroup and attach the supplied /64
concepts.text: Pair the eight resulting bytes into four IPv6 groups, then place those groups after the supplied network’s first four groups. Leading zeros may be omitted within a group. This changes the interface identifier, not the supplied network half. The worked table below shows every stage with separate practice values.

concepts.title: A correct address still needs a working route

worked.label: 1. Expand the six MAC bytes

worked.label: 2. Insert ff:fe and toggle 0x02
worked.value:
Inserted bytes:
00 16 3e ff fe 12 34 56
First byte: 00 XOR 02 = 02
Identifier bytes:
02 16 3e ff fe 12 34 56
worked.explanation: Only that one bit of the first byte flips. If it started as 1, it becomes 0; do not always set it.

worked.label: 3. Regroup and join the network half

Network half: fd64:7:0:0
ID: 0216:3eff:fe12:3456
Combined address/prefix:
fd64:7::216:3eff:fe12:3456/64

worked.label: 4. Verify the route as well
worked.value:
Destination: ::/0
Next hop: fe80::1
Outgoing interface: lan
Server: fd64:7:20::20

concepts.title: An endpoint starts or receives communication

concepts.title: A switch joins local Ethernet connections
concepts.text: Enabled ports on each supplied switch share one untagged network. Local Ethernet broadcasts can reach the other connected endpoints. A port name identifies a physical jack, not an IP address.

concepts.text: The router has one separately addressed interface on each side. It forwards IPv4 packets between those networks and supports the return path. Its two interfaces do not become one Ethernet network.

concepts.title: A document holds named settings
concepts.text: JSON is a text format for data. Curly braces group named values into an object. Double quotes mark text, including field names. A colon pairs each field name with its value, and commas separate fields.

concepts.title: Lists keep related records together
concepts.text: Square brackets hold an ordered list, called an array. Here switches is a list of switch records, and each ports list belongs to its enclosing switch. This application finds records by name, so reordering complete records keeps the same configuration.

concepts.title: Text, numbers and on/off values differ
concepts.text: A quoted value such as "p1" is text. The up field uses true or false without quotes. A VLAN ID is a number. This inventory requires an integer written with digits, from 1 to 4094; a quoted number or a decimal/exponent form is a field error. General JSON supports other number forms. The optional note accepts short text or null, meaning no note.

concepts.title: Apply and then check the behavior
concepts.text: Apply inventory reads the whole document and changes the simulated access ports only if it is valid. A rejected document leaves the prior applied settings active. Check network evaluates real simulated group paths and separation. A valid document can still describe the wrong VLAN or a down port.

concepts.title: An access point shares radio space
concepts.text: An access point connects Wi-Fi devices to a network. Its radio transmits in a frequency band. This activity uses only the 2.4 GHz band, with a fixed 20 MHz channel width. The channel number names the centre of that radio space; it is not a device address.

concepts.title: Different numbers can still overlap
concepts.text: Nearby channel centres are closer together than the width of a Wi-Fi channel. For this supplied site, use the conventional channels 1, 6 and 11. They provide separated choices in this plan; choosing 2 instead of 1 does not automatically avoid overlap. Other bands, widths and country plans need different decisions.

concepts.title: A survey shows which radios hear each other

goal: Configure WPA2-Personal and diagnose method, passphrase and profile-compatibility mistakes.
context: Builds on exact network names and enabled WLANs. This task keeps those supplied settings fixed and introduces personal security and management-frame compatibility.

concepts.title: Personal security uses a shared passphrase
concepts.text: WPA2-Personal lets devices use a shared passphrase instead of a separate account for each person. Enter only the fictional training value supplied with this lesson. It is not a password you use elsewhere.

concepts.title: The method must match the profile
concepts.text: A saved profile that requires WPA2-Personal will not accept the unfinished Open setting. WPA2-Personal uses a pre-shared key (PSK), derived from the shared passphrase, and a data-protection method called AES-CCMP. This simulator checks configuration compatibility without encrypting traffic.

concepts.title: The passphrase is exact input
concepts.text: The shared text is used to derive keys on real equipment. Here, the supplied values must match exactly: case and spaces matter. Use the supplied 8–63 character training value; this activity supports ordinary English letters, numbers, spaces and punctuation.

concepts.title: Management frames have a separate protection policy
concepts.text: Management frames help maintain a Wi-Fi connection. Protected management frames, or PMF, are separate from protecting ordinary data. Optional can protect a capable profile while permitting an older profile; Required refuses a profile that cannot offer PMF.

concepts.title: Verify intended access and intended refusal
concepts.text: A correct plan must satisfy the site policy and every supplied profile. Making one laptop work is insufficient if the scanner fails, a stale passphrase becomes compatible, or the visitor WLAN changes.

concepts.title: WPA3-Personal uses a different method
concepts.text: A shared passphrase can still be the text entered by the user, but WPA3-Personal uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, or SAE. It is not a renamed WPA2-PSK checkbox. The supplied profile must allow the actual method.

concepts.title: Protected management frames are required
concepts.text: WPA3-only requires PMF. Set the management-frame policy to Required together with WPA3-Personal. An optional policy is an incomplete WPA3-only configuration in this model.

concepts.title: A planned refusal can be correct
concepts.text: The modern profiles allow SAE. The retired scanner allows only WPA2-PSK and must not become compatible with this WPA3-only WLAN. Its expected refusal is different from an unexpected modern-client failure.

concepts.title: Keep other settings and users intact
concepts.text: Changing security must not rename the WLAN, replace its supplied training value or alter the visitor network. Check every supplied profile after changes; compatibility is a configuration result, not a measured radio connection.

goal: Repair central staff forwarding without disturbing management, visitor service or VLAN separation.
context: Builds on VLAN access/trunk/native classification and supplied Wi-Fi profiles. This unit studies provided same-LAN forwarding paths; radio, authentication and IP configuration are supplied.

concepts.title: An access point has two kinds of traffic
concepts.text: An access point (AP) connects wireless clients to the wired network. A wireless LAN controller (WLC) manages compatible APs. Management traffic between them and client data are different paths, even when they share a cable. Client security and addressing are supplied here; you are repairing VLAN forwarding.

concepts.title: Local AP mode is not local switching
concepts.text: In Cisco Local AP mode, client data leaves through the controller. A FlexConnect AP can instead use the WLAN’s local-switching setting to put client data onto its own wired connection. “Local mode” and “local switching” therefore do not mean the same thing.

concepts.title: Carry the VLAN where data actually leaves
concepts.text: In this Library example, the AP’s Access attachment carries management VLAN 110. Central client traffic leaves through the controller attachment, so its Trunk must carry staff VLAN 120 and visitor VLAN 130, as well as management. Repairing an unused AP data path would not repair the required controller path.

concepts.title: Verify service and separation together
concepts.text: A successful repair must deliver staff and visitor data in both directions, without sending staff data into the visitor service. Powering off or disconnecting a target is not proof of VLAN separation. Check paths evaluates the current topology, mappings and every supplied case.

worked.label: Management attachment
worked.explanation: Keep the supplied AP management-only Access connection. Client data is carried elsewhere in this design.

worked.label: AP mode
worked.explanation: Local AP mode sends client data through the controller, even if a WLAN permits local switching.

worked.label: Controller Trunk
worked.explanation: The controller needs the management VLAN and both client VLANs on its attachment.

worked.label: Staff path
worked.explanation: Both the outward and return paths must retain the staff VLAN.

worked.label: Preserved visitor path
worked.explanation: Restoring staff must not remove visitors or allow staff data into the visitor VLAN.

worked.label: Another valid design
worked.explanation: A FlexConnect AP with central WLAN switching can satisfy this same required forwarding location. The controller Trunk still needs the VLANs.

practice.title: Choose where client data leaves
practice.action: In AP settings, choose Local under AP mode. Leave the supplied management/native value and read-only AP attachment unchanged.
practice.observe: Local AP mode uses the controller data path even when the staff WLAN permits local switching.

practice.title: Repair the controller attachment and check
practice.action: In access/controller-port, keep Trunk with native VLAN 110; change Allowed VLANs to 110,120,130. Or choose Fill worked configuration. Choose Check paths.
practice.observe: Expected: management and both services meet the requirements; staff remains separated from visitors. Read the actual case results after checking.

practice.title: Try the permitted alternative
practice.action: Choose FlexConnect under AP mode and check with staff forwarding still Local. Then choose Central for the staff WLAN and check again.
practice.observe: The management-only AP Access port cannot carry tagged local client data in this activity. Central WLAN switching restores the controller path and is a valid alternative.

goal: Restore branch-local staff traffic while retaining centrally forwarded visitor service.
context: Builds on VLAN access/trunk/native classification and supplied Wi-Fi profiles. This unit studies provided same-LAN forwarding paths; radio, authentication and IP configuration are supplied.

concepts.title: Keep management and client VLANs separate
concepts.text: This Workshop AP uses native management VLAN 140. Native means untagged on its wired attachment: the AP and switch must agree on that number. Staff data uses VLAN 150; visitor data uses VLAN 160. A working management VLAN does not automatically carry either client VLAN.

concepts.title: Local switching needs a suitable AP mode
concepts.text: AP Local mode forwards client data through the controller. For staff data to leave at the branch AP, use FlexConnect with the staff WLAN’s Local forwarding setting. The visitor WLAN can continue using Central forwarding on the same AP.

concepts.title: Map the WLAN and carry its tag
concepts.text: The local staff WLAN must map to VLAN 150, and the AP’s Trunk must allow that VLAN. A mapping selects the client group; an allowed list permits its frames across the wire. Correcting only one of those two settings leaves the path broken.

concepts.title: Preserve the controller-forwarded visitors
concepts.text: Visitor VLAN 160 still leaves through the controller’s supplied Trunk. Keep that path working while changing staff settings. Check both forward and return paths and the required staff/visitor separation, not just the AP mode label.

worked.label: Management agreement
worked.explanation: Matching untagged management values restore the supplied transport. This is not a live controller-join test.

worked.label: AP mode
worked.explanation: FlexConnect permits per-WLAN local or central forwarding.

worked.label: Staff mapping
worked.explanation: Client frames leave at the AP using the staff VLAN.

worked.label: AP Trunk
worked.explanation: The native management VLAN and tagged local staff VLAN need to be carried. Preserve the other supplied VLAN.

worked.label: Visitor path
worked.explanation: Keep the visitor mapping and controller attachment unchanged.

worked.label: Verify all cases
worked.explanation: A disconnected destination or a native-VLAN leak is not a valid repair.

practice.observe: Management agreement is separate from staff forwarding. The supplied staff mapping is still wrong at this point.

practice.observe: A correct mapping cannot cross a Trunk that excludes its VLAN. AP Local mode changes the staff forwarding location even when the WLAN still says Local.

goal: Monitor an unexpected uplink failure without turning planned maintenance into an alarm.
context: Builds on network devices and TCP/UDP conversations. The supplied virtual agents are ready; this unit studies read-only measurements and monitor policy, not agent installation or live SNMP security.

concepts.title: A device can report its own measurements
concepts.text: A device agent reports measurements to a management application. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is one standard way to request them. Here the agent is a supplied virtual record, so you can investigate without connecting to equipment. A collection of named measurement definitions is called a management information base, or MIB.

concepts.title: Read the measurement and its row
concepts.text: An object identifier (OID) names a measurement. It is a dotted sequence of numbers, not an IPv4 address. GET reads one exact object. GETNEXT asks for the next object in numeric order. Starting at the ifDescr descriptions column lets a monitor discover interface rows rather than assume a fixed row number.

concepts.title: Intended state and observed state answer different questions
concepts.text: ifAdminStatus records whether an interface is intended to be Up. ifOperStatus records whether it is operationally Up. In this activity, 1 means Up and 2 means Down. An interface deliberately shut down can be operationally Down without being an unexpected failure.

concepts.title: Unknown is different from quiet
concepts.text: If the agent is unavailable or the interface name is absent, the monitor lacks evidence. It must report Unknown, not pretend the interface is healthy. A useful alert policy handles normal service, failures and planned maintenance together.

worked.label: Worked case
worked.explanation: Use a different virtual site from the independent assignment.

worked.label: Description and row
worked.explanation: GETNEXT through ifDescr finds the supplied description at this row; another sample can use a different row.

worked.label: ifAdminStatus.12
worked.explanation: The interface is intended to be available. GET numeric object ID 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.12 to read this example value.

worked.label: ifOperStatus.12
worked.explanation: The interface is not operationally available. GET numeric object ID 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.12 to read it; the final number is the discovered row.

worked.label: Monitor rule
worked.explanation: Together these states describe an unplanned link failure; raise an alert.

worked.label: Other required cases
worked.explanation: Do not suppress every alert or label missing evidence as a healthy link.

practice.observe: The browser shows an actual simulated response only after polling. The final number identifies that interface row.

practice.observe: The unexpected failure alerts; normal and planned shutdown stay quiet. Missing or unavailable measurements remain Unknown.

practice.title: Investigate a noisy rule
practice.action: Change Alert rule to Any operationally Down link and check again. Find the failing maintenance case, then restore the useful rule and check.
practice.observe: Operationally Down alone does not tell you whether a shutdown was planned.

goal: Repair an incoming-traffic monitor without inventing rates from interrupted or ambiguous measurements.
context: Builds on network devices and TCP/UDP conversations. The supplied virtual agents are ready; this unit studies read-only measurements and monitor policy, not agent installation or live SNMP security.

concepts.title: A counter is a total, not a speed
concepts.text: An octet is a byte: 8 bits. ifHCInOctets counts incoming octets over time; ifHCOutOctets counts outgoing octets. To measure traffic rate, subtract two compatible totals, multiply the difference by 8 and divide by elapsed seconds. The direction matters.

concepts.title: Use link capacity to interpret the rate
concepts.text: The worked workshop link has 100 Mbit/s capacity. Its incoming total grows by 175,000,000 octets over 20 seconds. Convert that growth to bits and divide by time: the result is 70 Mbit/s, or 70% of capacity. The worked table below shows each calculation. A 60% warning alerts for this busy case and stays quiet for the 20% case.

concepts.title: A short counter can hide complete turns
concepts.text: A 32-bit counter returns to zero after 4,294,967,296 octets. On a fast link, an interval can hide a complete turn, so two 32-bit values may not determine the rate. Use the high-capacity 64-bit object when that can happen. The slower, shorter worked example also permits 32-bit counters; do not assume they are always wrong.

concepts.title: Do not join incompatible measurements
concepts.text: A changed counter-discontinuity marker means the total was restarted. An inconsistent agent uptime, missing interface or unavailable sample also prevents a reliable comparison. Report Unknown rather than a made-up zero or a huge traffic spike.

worked.label: Supplied workshop input
worked.explanation: Use the link capacity and elapsed sample interval, not a guessed polling speed.

worked.label: Incoming total
worked.explanation: Subtract the earlier total from the current total: the increase is 175,000,000 octets. A total by itself is not a speed.

worked.label: Convert octets to bits
worked.explanation: Multiply the increase of 175,000,000 octets by 8 bits per octet.

worked.label: Divide by elapsed time
worked.explanation: Divide 1,400,000,000 bits by 20 seconds: the result is 70 Mbit/s.

worked.label: Compare with capacity
worked.explanation: A useful threshold separates this busy sample from the quiet 20% sample.

worked.label: Worked warning level
worked.explanation: This is one valid workshop policy, not the independent assignment’s answer.

worked.label: Interrupted measurements
worked.explanation: Keep unavailable, absent and restarted-counter cases distinct from ordinary quiet traffic.

practice.title: Compare two actual counter values
practice.action: Choose Sustained receive load. Enter 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.7 in Object ID and choose GET. Poll Earlier sample, then Current sample.
practice.observe: Expected for Sustained receive load: totals of 2,000 and 175,002,000 octets, an increase of 175,000,000 over 20 seconds. Compare those values with Actual query result; the derived rate is 70 Mbit/s.

practice.title: Configure useful incoming-traffic alerts
practice.action: Enter workshop-uplink as Interface description. Choose Incoming, 64-bit high-capacity, and 60 for Warning at %. Or choose Fill worked monitor. Choose Check monitor.
practice.observe: The busy sample alerts and the quiet sample does not. A counter restart, missing interface or unavailable agent gives Unknown.

practice.title: Change one choice and explain the result
practice.action: Choose Outgoing and check; compare the busy case. Restore Incoming, then try 32-bit counters on this short, slower example and check again.
practice.observe: Direction changes the measured traffic. Both counter widths work for this particular interval; the independent fast-link task needs you to reconsider that assumption.

Use only the displayed monitor settings; preserve all supplied agent measurements.

goal: Read a resource, diagnose authorization and JSON errors, then verify the network.
context: First complete JSON inventory and VLAN handover. This is a lab-defined controller; resource paths and identity labels do not contact real equipment.

concepts.title: Read before changing
concepts.text: A resource is a named piece of data. GET /profiles lists the profiles; GET /profiles/team reads one profile. A binding selects which profile controls a supplied port. Changing a shared profile affects every port using it.

concepts.title: A request has separate parts
concepts.text: Method says what to do; Path selects the resource; Authorization identifies who is asking; Content-Type describes the body. GET reads. PATCH changes named fields. PUT replaces the full representation, so include required fields and any description you need to retain.

concepts.title: Permission and JSON types matter
concepts.text: This simulator supplies Bearer lab-reader for reading and Bearer lab-operator for changes. A missing or invalid identity gets 401; a reader attempting a change gets 403. These labels are not real credentials. JSON true is an on/off value; "true" is text. PATCH uses application/merge-patch+json. A rejected request leaves resources unchanged.

concepts.title: Response success is not task success
concepts.text: Send request applies one valid change. A 204 response means this origin accepted the update; it does not prove the desired network works. Check network separately tests current paths, group separation and protected fields. Editing request fields clears the current result; sending a change can break a previously working network.

requirements: Restore communication between the two staff endpoints by repairing the staff profile.

practice.observe: The read identity cannot change a resource. After permission is fixed, wrong media type produces a different error; neither refusal changes the network.

practice.observe: The boolean enables both ports using team. All requirements should pass while guests remain separate and the description stays intact.

goal: Create, rebind, verify and retire resources while protecting another group.
context: Complete Repair an authorized network change request first. Reuse its JSON, permission and media-type skills while moving resources in this lab-defined controller.

concepts.title: Create data before choosing it
concepts.text: POST /profiles creates a named profile from name, up and vlan. A 201 response includes Location, the new resource path. PUT /profiles/NAME can also create a full profile at that path. Existing port bindings keep their old selection until you change them.

concepts.title: Move one binding at a time
concepts.text: GET /bindings lists port selections. PATCH /bindings/desk-3 with a new profile name changes only that port. Moving just one peer can split a working pair: a valid 204 response is not a complete handover.

concepts.title: Retire safely after verification
concepts.text: DELETE removes an unused profile. This origin returns 409 while a port still selects it, so read the bindings and move the remaining users first. The two guest ports need the target VLAN; staff must keep its existing profile and behavior.

concepts.title: Use replacement and partial changes deliberately
concepts.text: PUT replaces the whole resource representation; PATCH changes only named fields. PATCH description:null removes an optional description. Removing up, vlan or a binding profile is invalid because those fields are required. You may choose a different new profile name if its behavior meets the full assignment.

goal: Retrieve a server file into a new device name and verify the actual result.
requirements: Download Recovery/public/recovery.cfg to Device/staged.cfg using the supplied TFTP service.
Keep Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt and the published recovery file unchanged.
Keep the TFTP transfer path ready across all supplied files and transfer ports. A staged file is not an activated configuration.
context: A server supplies files; a client requests an operation. Here Device is the client. You have already explored IP endpoints and UDP in the transport unit; no terminal command or equipment setup is needed.

concepts.title: Read the direction from the device’s point of view
concepts.text: Download brings a server file onto the device. Upload sends a device file to the server. The two file fields always name Device and Server stores; changing direction changes which one is read and which one is written.

concepts.title: TFTP uses a request, data blocks and replies
concepts.text: The client sends its first request to UDP port 69. Data and acknowledgements then use the client and server transfer ports shown in Sample inputs. Each data block must be acknowledged; UDP alone does not guarantee delivery. This exercise uses byte-preserving octet mode. TFTP has no directory-listing command; use the file inventory supplied by this task.

concepts.title: A copy is not the same as a correct handover
concepts.text: Copy into a new file name so you retain the current configuration. Then inspect the new file and check the task: a successful transfer can still copy an outdated file. TFTP has no login and no encryption in this exercise; these are nonsecret training files.

worked.label: Direction
worked.explanation: Read a file supplied by the server; do not upload a device file.

worked.label: Server file
worked.explanation: This is the published training replacement, not public/retired.cfg.

goal: Make an FTP archive copy work while preserving the original files and a blocked service.
requirements: Upload Device/current.cfg to Archive/archive/branch.cfg through FTP using a supplied write-capable training login.
Repair only R1’s supplied router policy so control and every listed passive data endpoint work in both directions.
Preserve Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt and Archive/archive/audit.cfg. Keep Telnet traffic to Archive blocked.
Verify exact archived bytes and the current transfer path across all supplied inputs.
context: The transport unit taught TCP openings, source/service ports and the native ACL document. This task adds a file operation on top. Training logins are provided choices, not real accounts or credentials.

concepts.title: Control and file data use different connections
concepts.text: FTP first opens a TCP control connection to server port 21. A successful control connection or login does not prove that file data can move. In passive mode the server supplies another listening port; the client opens that separate TCP data connection.

concepts.title: Connection direction and file direction are different
concepts.text: For this upload, Device opens both connections and sends the file. For a download, the client still opens a passive data connection, but the server sends the file bytes back. Read both source and destination ports when repairing the return policy.

concepts.title: A login can have limited permission
concepts.text: reader can inspect archive files but cannot publish a new one. archivist and backup-operator can write files under archive/. This models named-profile admission and file permission, not a real authentication exchange. Plain FTP does not encrypt these training transfers.

concepts.title: Repair the useful path without removing protection
concepts.text: Use Sample inputs to find all passive endpoints, not only the first one. Add the necessary narrow rules before the deny. Keep Telnet blocked and retain the supplied files; permitting everything is not a successful handover.

worked.label: Operation
worked.explanation: Upload preserves the local source and creates the server archive.

worked.label: Control connection
worked.value: Client 49152 → server TCP 21, with its reverse reply
worked.explanation: This already works in the practice starter.

worked.label: Passive data endpoints
worked.value: Server TCP 53010–53012; replies return to client 49152
worked.explanation: The additional connection needs rules in both directions.

worked.label: Training login
worked.explanation: Both supplied profiles can write archive/; reader cannot.

practice.title: Reproduce the data failure
practice.action: Select Transfer file without changing the starter. Open Packet and file stages under Actual transfer, then read the control, login and data-connection stages.
practice.observe: Control and login pass, but the passive data opening is filtered. No archive file is created.

practice.title: Apply the worked repair

practice.observe: The rules allow the listed passive range in both directions while keeping the final deny. The archive contains the original current.cfg bytes.

practice.title: Separate permission from connectivity
practice.action: Change Training login to reader and transfer again. Read the feedback, then choose another supplied write-capable login and retry.
practice.observe: A working connection does not grant write access. The failed request leaves the archive untouched; either supported writer can complete the task.

goal: Archive the original file and stage its replacement without confusing their contents.
requirements: Upload Device/current.cfg to Archive/archive/original.cfg using FTP and a supplied write-capable training login.
Download Recovery/public/recovery.cfg to Device/staged.cfg using TFTP. The staged replacement must not be archived as the original.
Preserve Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt, Archive/archive/audit.cfg and Recovery/public/recovery.cfg.
Repair only R1’s router policy. Keep both transfer paths ready for every listed endpoint and retain the Telnet restriction to Archive.
context: Complete the recovery-copy and passive-FTP lessons first if these roles are new. Both assignments remain visible here: the archive needs the original bytes, while the staged file needs the replacement bytes.

concepts.title: Keep original and replacement roles separate
concepts.text: An archive preserves what is stored now. A staged replacement is a different file waiting for a later decision. Copying the staged file into an archive named original does not make it the original; check actual contents rather than labels.

concepts.title: Choose the service for each server
concepts.text: Archive offers FTP with supplied write-capable login profiles and a separate passive data endpoint. Recovery offers read-only TFTP with no login. Use the service shown for that server and read upload/download from the device’s point of view.

concepts.title: A handover includes preserved work and a ready path
concepts.text: Two copied files are only part of the task. Keep current.cfg and the audit file unchanged, support every supplied transfer endpoint and retain the denied service. A repair that works for only the first sample is incomplete.

concepts.title: Verify before activating anything
concepts.text: Inspect the two destinations and compare them with their intended sources. This lab stages and archives files only; it does not activate configurations. FTP and TFTP in this exercise are unencrypted and use nonsecret training data.

worked.label: Archive original
worked.explanation: Use the original local file as the archive source.

worked.label: Stage replacement
worked.explanation: Use a new local file name; leave current.cfg intact.

worked.label: Connection paths
worked.value: FTP control 21 + passive 53010–53012; TFTP request 69 + transfer 53020–53022
worked.explanation: Use the supplied client port 49152 and retain the matching reverse paths.

worked.label: Verify independently
worked.value: Original archive and replacement stage are different byte strings
worked.explanation: The order can vary because neither operation changes current.cfg.

practice.observe: Only the original local file is archived. The staged-file requirement is still unfinished; a partial handover is not completion.

practice.action: Select TFTP and Gallery, then Fill worked transfer and Transfer file. Inspect lesson.cfg and the archive, then Check example.
practice.observe: The staged bytes come from Gallery, while the archive still contains the original current.cfg. Both sample paths and protections pass.

practice.action: Select FTP, Upload and PracticeVault. Choose Training login archivist or backup-operator. Change Device file to lesson.cfg and Server file to archive/demo.cfg, then Transfer file and Check example. Restore current.cfg as the upload source and retry.
practice.observe: The upload itself succeeds, but the archive requirement explains that the replacement is not the original. A later correct transfer repairs the result without a reset.

goal: Restore independent campus uplinks and prove the stated structural outage paths.
context: Prerequisite: complete the wired-device cable and routed-path lessons, or use their concepts of devices, ports and cable endpoints. This unit teaches campus roles with already-configured routed links.

concepts.title: Start with the access layer
concepts.text: An access device is where a group of users connects. North and South represent two access groups. Their upstream devices join those groups; another access device is not a transit shortcut in this exercise.

concepts.title: Combine two jobs in a small campus
concepts.text: In a two-tier design, the upper layer does both distribution (joining access groups) and core (carrying traffic across the campus) jobs. The diagram labels those devices Distribution + core. Two-tier describes roles, not exactly two switches.

concepts.title: Check what happens when a device is lost
concepts.text: Two cables to one upper device both depend on that device. Connect to two different upper devices, then inspect the stated outages. A structural path assumes its routed links are already configured; it does not prove IP forwarding or measure recovery time.

requirements: Connect each access device to two different combined distribution/core devices. Two cables to the same device are not two independent uplinks.
Complete every supplied cable; use each physical port at most once and keep the two protected cables unchanged.
Keep a hierarchy path between North access and South access with all devices available, with West combined unavailable, and with East combined unavailable.

practice.title: Count different parent devices
practice.action: Select Check answers on the starter. Beside cable ne, inspect its End 2: it repeats Guide West combined. The failed rows identify the missing independent uplink.
practice.observe: The normal path can pass while a device-loss case or a parent-count requirement fails.

practice.title: Repair the two upper endpoints
practice.action: Set ne End 2 to Guide East combined / p1. Set se End 2 to Guide East combined / p2. Select Check answers.
practice.observe: Both access devices now have two distinct upstream devices, and the stated outage paths pass.

practice.title: Explore an outage without changing the cables
practice.action: Select Guide East combined unavailable under Inspect a stated case. Inspect the path through West. Then unplug ne End 2 and check again; repair it afterward.
practice.observe: Selecting a case changes the observation only. Editing a cable clears the previous check, even if the selected case still has a path.

worked.label: Independent upper connections
worked.value:
North -> West + East
South -> West + East
worked.explanation: Each access device uses two different combined distribution/core devices.

worked.label: Normal and failed-device observations
worked.value:
Normal: North -> West -> South
West lost: North -> East -> South
worked.explanation: The alternate path depends on both access groups having a cable to East. The table below lets you build that wiring in separate practice.

goal: Repair a three-tier campus’s building links and redundant core paths.
context: Prerequisite: complete the wired-device cable and routed-path lessons, or use their concepts of devices, ports and cable endpoints. This unit teaches campus roles with already-configured routed links.

concepts.title: Give each building a distribution block
concepts.text: Access switches connect to distribution devices in their own building. Distribution collects the local access links and provides the next hop toward other buildings. The building label is part of this exercise’s required organization.

concepts.title: Use a separate core between blocks
concepts.text: A dedicated core joins the distribution blocks. A normal cross-building path is Access, local Distribution, Core, remote Distribution, then Access. This is different from a small collapsed-core design, where the upper devices perform both jobs.

concepts.title: Repair organization and resilience
concepts.text: Physical connectivity alone can hide a misplaced access cable or a single remaining upstream device. Check the actual role path and each stated core/distribution outage. These are structural routed-adjacency checks, not STP, IP policy, timing or a universal campus-design rule.

requirements: Connect each access device only to distribution devices in its own named building. Keep two different upstream devices for every access and distribution device.
Complete all supplied cables without sharing a physical port. Edit only a-dn1, a-ds1, w-dn2 and e-ds2; preserve the other cable endpoints.
Keep a hierarchy path from North access to South access with all devices available and after each stated single core or distribution device outage.

practice.title: Separate a physical path from the right building path
practice.action: Select Check answers. Inspect a-dn1 and a-ds1: their distribution endpoints belong to the opposite buildings. Compare the role/building row and the case rows.
practice.observe: A physically connected layout can fail the required hierarchy. Each access device must use its local distribution block.

practice.title: Repair access and core endpoints
practice.action: Set a-dn1 End 2 to Guide North distribution A / p1 and a-ds1 End 2 to Guide South distribution A / p1. Connect w-dn2 End 2 to Guide West core / p2 and e-ds2 End 2 to Guide East core / p4. Select Check answers.
practice.observe: The independent-parent counts and all seven normal/outage cases pass. These are the separate example’s ports, not a populated assignment.

practice.title: Inspect why redundancy matters
practice.action: Choose one distribution-unavailable case. Follow the remaining path. Unplug an editable core cable, check again, then restore it.
practice.observe: The failing rows name the particular outage that loses a path. A normal path by itself cannot earn completion.

worked.label: Local collection
worked.value:
North -> North A + North B
South -> South A + South B
worked.explanation: In the separate Guide equipment, North A/B and South A/B are the named local distribution devices.

worked.label: Separate campus transit
worked.value:
North -> North A -> West core
West core -> South A -> South
worked.explanation: Each distribution device also connects to both cores. If a stated device is unavailable, the path is derived from the remaining chosen links.

goal: Commission a new rack while preserving independent internal spine paths.
context: Prerequisite: campus access/distribution/core roles and cable endpoints. A rack holds computers; its leaf switch connects them to the fabric. This task starts with routed links already configured.

concepts.title: Give each rack a leaf; connect every leaf to every spine
concepts.text: A leaf connects a rack to the shared upper switches, called spines. In this conventional two-tier shape, leaves do not connect directly to other leaves, and spines do not connect directly to other spines. Each leaf has a separate connection to every supplied spine.

concepts.title: Count the shared middle devices
concepts.text: A path between two leaves goes from the first leaf, through a shared available spine, to the second leaf: two cables. In the separate guide equipment, two shared spines give two internal alternatives. Two parallel cables to the same spine still depend on that one spine.

concepts.title: Add a rack without weakening the existing fabric
concepts.text: Keep the existing rack connections intact. Connect the new leaf to all supplied spines, then select each unavailable-spine case and inspect the actual rack pair. With two guide spines, one loss should leave one alternative. The independent assignment uses three spines and asks for two remaining alternatives after one loss.

requirements: Commission Rack 4 by completing its three supplied cables. Connect every leaf to three different spines; use each port at most once and preserve all nine existing rack cables.

Keep three distinct internal spine alternatives from each existing rack to Rack 4 with all devices available, and at least two after each stated single-spine loss. A parallel cable to one spine does not count as another spine.

practice.title: Inspect the missing rack connections
practice.action: Select Check answers. In the cable table, r3-s1 and r3-s2 have unplugged second ends. Inspect the stated normal case and the rack-pair selector.
practice.observe: The new rack has no shared spine paths. Existing rack links remain protected, so the work is to commission the new leaf.

practice.title: Commission the separate guide rack
practice.action: Set r3-s1 End 2 to Guide Spine 1 / p3 and r3-s2 End 2 to Guide Spine 2 / p3. Select Check answers.
practice.observe: Both guide rack pairs have two distinct internal spine alternatives normally and one after either spine is unavailable. The displayed observation follows the selected pair and case.

practice.title: Test and recover a missing alternative
practice.action: Unplug r3-s2 End 2. Check answers, then choose Guide Spine 1 unavailable. Read the failing pair feedback; reconnect the cable and check again.
practice.observe: One normal path can remain while the full task fails. After the only connected spine is unavailable, no path remains. Reconnecting clears old checks until you check the repaired layout.

worked.label: Guide rack fan-out
worked.explanation: Separate guide Rack 3 needs one unused port on each spine. Its two editable cables use the same device roles as the existing rack connections.

worked.label: Guide internal alternatives
worked.value:
Rack 1 -> Spine 1 -> Rack 3
Rack 1 -> Spine 2 -> Rack 3
worked.explanation: Two distinct internal spines normally; one when either spine is unavailable. Rack endpoints and cables can still be shared, so this is not a claim of fully disjoint end-to-end paths.

goal: Repair placement so both services stay ready when any one physical host is unavailable.
context: Prerequisites: VLAN/IPv4 and campus device-role foundations. An operating system manages a computer; its kernel is the core that manages hardware. This exercise supplies compatible hypervisors and guest operating systems. You are placing represented workloads, not starting actual guests.

concepts.title: A VM brings its own operating-system kernel
concepts.text: A hypervisor supplies virtual hardware for a guest operating system. The VM has its own kernel. The supplied hypervisors support every listed guest operating system, so a FreeBSD guest can use the guide’s Windows host; that host still needs a hypervisor.

concepts.title: A Linux container shares its host’s kernel
concepts.text: A container isolates a process environment and its files while sharing the host kernel. These Linux containers need a Linux host with a supplied container runtime. That is different from selecting a VM guest kernel.

concepts.title: Separate replicas before a host fails
concepts.text: A replica is another copy of the same service workload. Copies on one physical host all depend on it. Keep at least one copy on another compatible host and respect the stated memory/CPU-unit planning budgets. These are exercise policies, not performance predictions or universal overcommit rules.

worked.label: Guide VM
worked.explanation: Its listed guest operating system is compatible with the supplied hypervisors, including the Windows spare host.

worked.label: Guide container
worked.explanation: It needs alpha or beta: a Linux kernel and runtime. spare supplies neither for this container.

worked.label: Failure domain
worked.explanation: Any workload placed on alpha becomes unavailable in that experiment; another host must retain a replica of each service.

practice.title: Repair kernel/runtime compatibility
practice.action: In Workload placement, move status-a off spare to a supplied Linux runtime host. Select Run experiment with all hosts available.
practice.observe: Actual observation names each workload and explains readiness or the failed compatibility/budget.

practice.title: Try a physical-host outage
practice.action: Select alpha unavailable and Run experiment. Spread the archive and status service replicas across compatible hosts, then run each single-host outage.
practice.observe: A normally ready VM still becomes unavailable with its host. At least one copy of each service should remain ready.

practice.title: Check the whole guide plan
practice.action: Select Check answers. If a group fails an outage case, use its named host and service to revisit placement, then retry.
practice.observe: Example checks pass only after normal readiness and every required single-host outage; the independent task uses its own names and draft.

goal: Repair a virtual port and an uplink without merging tenant networks.
context: Use the existing VLAN foundation first. A virtual switch provides Layer 2 forwarding inside a represented host; its uplink joins the physical network. No VM or hypervisor is required on your computer.

concepts.title: A virtual NIC is the VM’s network adapter
concepts.text: A VM sees a network adapter even though its switching connection can be software inside the physical host. In this lesson each supplied VM is cabled to a named virtual-switch port.

concepts.title: Local and cross-host paths are different
concepts.text: A virtual switch can join local virtual adapters. To reach a VM on another host, traffic also crosses its host uplink, the supplied physical switch and the other host’s uplink. A missing allowed VLAN breaks that longer path.

concepts.title: Keep service and separation together
concepts.text: Repairing a path must not merge accounting and visitor groups. Verify that each intended pair can exchange broadcasts and that unwanted pairs remain separated. Stopping a port is not a valid substitute.

worked.label: Virtual NIC attachment
worked.explanation: The virtual adapter’s access VLAN determines its local group.

worked.label: Cross-host uplink
worked.explanation: Its allowed list must carry studio30 as well as visitor40; a correct VM port cannot replace this link policy.

worked.label: Observe after repair
worked.explanation: Inspect broadcast delivery must show the other intended VM without visitor recipients.

goal: Repair interface membership and identify which same-numbered endpoint actually replied.
context: Prerequisites: IPv4 static-forwarding, VLAN and campus foundations. A routing table tells a router where to send an address. VRF means a separate routing-table context inside the same physical router; it is different from a VLAN’s Layer 2 grouping.

concepts.title: One router can hold separate routing tables
concepts.text: Each interface belongs to one context, so its connected network appears in that context’s table. This lesson keeps addresses fixed and uses connected routes only; the context names are arbitrary labels.

concepts.title: Separate tenants can reuse an address plan
concepts.text: The studio and visitor guide networks use the same IP numbers. Keep each tenant’s client-side and server-side interfaces together in one context and the other tenant in the other context. Putting both copies in one table creates duplicate addresses.

concepts.title: An address reply is not an endpoint identity
concepts.text: When two tenants reuse numbers, a successful address probe can reach a different named device. Inspect Actual observation: it names the requested endpoint, actual destination and the router context used. Correct service and separation both matter.

worked.label: Guide studio context
worked.explanation: These two interfaces carry the studio client and server; their connected routes share a table.

worked.label: Guide visitor context
worked.explanation: The same numeric subnets are safe here because they belong to a separate table.

worked.label: Same-numbered reply
worked.explanation: The address can answer at studio-server instead. That is not access to visitor-server; endpoint identity distinguishes them.

practice.title: Separate the duplicate guide address plans
practice.action: In the interface context selectors, keep both studio interfaces in one context and both visitor interfaces in the other. Either context name may serve either group.
practice.observe: Duplicate-address feedback goes away when copies live in different routing tables.

practice.title: Inspect the intended path and a misleading reply
practice.action: Choose studio-client and studio-server, then Run experiment. Change Intended endpoint to visitor-server and run again.
practice.observe: The first reaches studio-server. The second may answer at the same-numbered studio-server, explicitly labeled as a different endpoint.

practice.title: Verify the complete guide policy
practice.action: Select Check answers; inspect any named failed pair, adjust the interface contexts and retry. Leave the router available.
practice.observe: All intended pairs and cross-tenant separation cases must pass. Turning the router off cannot satisfy the positive paths.

requirements: Keep the router available and each tenant’s client/server pair able to reach its intended partner and reply.
Keep east and west in separate routing contexts on shared-edge while preserving their supplied, overlapping addresses.
Either supplied context name can serve either tenant. A same-numbered reply from the wrong endpoint does not count as the requested path.
